value.body: Writes the low-level code that runs directly on chips inside devices — the software that starts a board, drives its sensors and peripherals, and handles updates. Employers include semiconductor companies, consumer-electronics, automotive and IoT product firms, and engineering-services companies. A day involves writing C code, reading datasheets and register maps, and debugging on real hardware.

items.label: Common tools
items.value: C, assembly basics, JTAG debuggers, Git, oscilloscope

items.label: Typical work
items.value: Bootloaders, device drivers, RTOS tasks, firmware updates

value.title: How you get in
value.body: The usual route is campus hiring into a semiconductor, automotive or engineering-services company, or a trainee role at a product startup. Strong C, computer-architecture basics and personal projects on microcontroller boards matter most at interviews. A post-graduate diploma in embedded systems is a common bridge for graduates of other branches.

value.title: Skills you'll use
items: C programming with pointers and memory management
Hardware debugging with JTAG and oscilloscopes

value.title: At a glance
items: A close cousin of embedded systems engineering; many job ads use both titles.
Growth path: firmware engineer → senior → lead or architect, or a move into embedded Linux, kernel or security work.
Bugs can be hard to reproduce, so careful testing is a large part of the job.
